Basal metabolic rate measurements in the Andean Altiplano mouse (Abrothrix andinus) have been derived from controlled respirometry trials conducted under standard thermoneutral conditions. At a core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], the maximum resting oxygen consumption recorded for this species is 64.7 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 64.7 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that reflects the elevated metabolic demands associated with life in the cold, high-altitude puna grasslands of the central Andes. This measurement is notably higher than what would be predicted for a rodent of its body size based on general allometric equations, suggesting that Abrothrix andinus has evolved a relatively high basal thermogenic capacity to cope with the severe nocturnal temperature drops characteristic of its habitat. Comparative data from related sigmodontine rodents indicate that this level of oxygen consumption is consistent with a strategy of sustained endothermy under hypoxic conditions, where efficient oxygen delivery and heat production are critical for survival. The metabolic physiology of this species thus provides a compelling example of adaptation to extreme environmental gradients.

Newborn pups of the Andean Altiplano mouse are altricial and weigh approximately 2.4 grams [Wwb = approximately 2.4 grams] at birth, a modest mass typical of small-bodied murid rodents that invest heavily in rapid postnatal growth. This neonatal mass is similar to that documented in the closely related Akodon azarae and represents a considerable maternal investment given the harsh, resource-limited environments these mice inhabit. Females typically produce litters of 5 pups [N_R_i = litters of 5 pups] per reproductive event, and under the stable thermal conditions of the laboratory, maintained at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], they can achieve approximately 2.5 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 2.5 litters per year], an annual reproductive output that balances relatively small litter size with moderate breeding frequency. This pattern is consistent with a life-history strategy emphasizing repeated, modest reproductive bouts rather than a single, large seasonal pulse, an adaptation that buffers against the stochasticity of food availability and extreme weather events in the high Andes.

The gestation period in Abrothrix andinus has been estimated at 22.7 days [tg = 22.7 days] when females are maintained at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], a duration that falls within the typical range for small-bodied sigmodontine rodents and is consistent with values reported for Akodon azarae. Following parturition, the neonates undergo a period of intense dependency during which they rely entirely on maternal milk. At a core temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], the time since birth at weaning is approximately 14.5 days since birth [tx = approximately 14.5 days since birth], after which the young begin to consume solid food and become nutritionally independent. This relatively brief weaning period is typical of rodents that experience high juvenile mortality, where rapid development to independence confers a selective advantage by reducing the window of vulnerability to predation. The synchronized progression from gestation through weaning underscores the tightly regulated developmental schedule that enables this species to exploit ephemeral resource pulses in its unpredictable alpine environment.

Sexual maturation in the Andean Altiplano mouse occurs relatively early in life, a pattern commonly observed in small mammals with high extrinsic mortality rates. Under laboratory conditions at a core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], puberty is attained at 60 days since birth [tp = 60 days since birth], a value that aligns with estimates for related Akodon species and suggests that individuals can become reproductively active within their first season of birth if conditions are favorable. The attainment of maximum adult body mass, or ultimate wet weight, is reported at 34.6 grams [Wwi = 34.6 grams], although field surveys and museum records from the GBIF database indicate that free-living individuals more commonly range between 12 and 17 grams, likely reflecting the energetic constraints of foraging in a sparse, high-altitude landscape where food resources are seasonally limited. Captive individuals, by contrast, often achieve the upper end of this mass range due to ad libitum feeding and the absence of thermoregulatory stress. This disparity between field and laboratory masses highlights the significant impact of ecological conditions on somatic growth trajectories in this species.

Longevity data for Abrothrix andinus remain sparse, but estimates based on the closely related Akodon molinae suggest a maximum lifespan of approximately 4 years [am = approximately 4 years] when maintained at a stable core temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], a duration that is relatively long for a small rodent and implies a slow pace of aging compared to many muroid species of similar body mass. The interaction between reproductive timing and survival is particularly relevant in this context: individuals that reach puberty at 60 days since birth [tp = 60 days since birth] and achieve their first successful breeding event soon thereafter can, over a four-year lifespan, accumulate numerous litters, each consisting of 5 pups [N_R_i = each consisting of 5 pups], and with females capable of producing up to 2.5 litters per year [F_R_i = up to 2.5 litters per year] at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This demographic profile, characterized by a relatively long lifespan, early maturation, and sustained moderate fecundity, is well suited to the unpredictable cold environments of the Andean Altiplano, where years of poor resource availability may be interspersed with brief periods of high productivity.
